title: Hazardous Materials Operations
summary: Recognize, isolate, deny entry, use current references, and take defensive actions within operations-level training — not technician work.

skills.title: Recognition and Identification
skills.summary: Use clues, markings, occupancy, and current references to identify likely hazards without becoming part of the release.
skills.whyItMatters: Wrong ID produces wrong isolation and dead firefighters. Guessing a product from a smell is not a tactic.
learningPoints: Occupancy, container shape, placards/labels, shipping papers, and people are clues — not certainties.
Stay out of the product. Binoculars beat footsteps.
The ERG is a starting reference, not a chemistry degree.
If clues conflict, isolate wider and call resources.

terminology.meaning: Diamond marking on bulk transport giving hazard class clues.
Documents that may name the product — obtained without becoming a victim.

safetyNotes: Do not walk into a cloud to read a 4-digit number.
Terrorism/WMD clues change isolation and notifications.

seeResources.label: HazMat Placard Reference
seeResources.note: Class clues for training — verify with a current official source.

drill.objective: From photos or a training trailer, list clues, state what you will not do, and locate the correct ERG guide concept without entering the hot zone.
drill.equipment: Current ERG, photos or props, binoculars if available.
drill.setup: Stay at a conservative distance. No product.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Name five clue categories before you mention a chemical name.
debrief: What if there is no placard?

15.title: 15-minute ERG drill
15.instructions: Three IDs: UN number, placard-only, occupancy-only. Find the guide page idea and isolation concept.
debrief: When do we upgrade to a tech team?

30.title: 30-minute scene problem
30.instructions: Mixed clues (facility + vehicle). Build a notification and isolation recommendation.
commonMistakes: Declaring the product from a smell
debrief: What did we still not know?

readinessQuestions.q: The safest way to get a 4-digit ID is often:
choices: Use optics, papers from a safe person, or facility staff — not your lungs
readinessQuestions.why: Distance is a tactic.

readinessQuestions.q: If occupancy says pesticide and the placard says flammable liquid:
choices: Treat the uncertainty as a reason for wider isolation and specialist help
readinessQuestions.why: Conflicting clues are a warning.

readinessQuestions.q: FireOpsSim placard pages are:
choices: A replacement for the current ERG
Training aids — confirm with the current official ERG and SOP
readinessQuestions.why: References go out of date.

skills.title: Isolation and Protective Actions
skills.summary: Establish initial isolation, deny entry, and choose protective actions from current references and the AHJ plan.
skills.whyItMatters: Most lives at a HazMat scene are saved by keeping people out of the product, not by heroic entries.
learningPoints: Initial isolation is a conservative guess you can enlarge.
Evacuate vs shelter-in-place depends on the material, building, and time.
Control the people problem: spectators, employees, and your own crews.
Weather (wind) is part of the geometry.
beforeYouDo: Current ERG isolation/protective action tables as applicable.

terminology.meaning: Stop additional people from walking into the problem.
Evacuate or shelter-in-place decisions for the public.

safetyNotes: Do not place engines in the plume to ‘block the road.’
Your isolation is not a technician’s hot-zone tape — but it must still be real.

drill.objective: On a map, set an initial isolation polygon using wind and a current reference concept, then identify who is still inside it.
drill.equipment: Map, cones if outdoor, current ERG, radios.
drill.setup: Tabletop is fine. Use today’s wind if outdoors.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Upwind, uphill, upstream — say it and place the first engine.
debrief: Who do we move first?

15.title: 15-minute map problem
15.instructions: School, highway, and a small leak. Pick evacuate vs shelter for one building.
debrief: What changed when the wind shifted?

30.title: 30-minute expanding incident
30.instructions: Start small, then a larger release inject. Re-draw isolation and notifications.
commonMistakes: Holding a tiny circle for pride
debrief: When is this bigger than Ops-level?

readinessQuestions.q: Initial isolation should be:
choices: Conservative and adjustable as information improves
readinessQuestions.why: You can shrink later more easily than you can un-expose people.

readinessQuestions.q: Shelter-in-place can be better than evacuation when:
choices: You want to ignore the public
The atmosphere outside is worse and buildings can protect people for a time
readinessQuestions.why: It is a timed, informed choice — not a default.

readinessQuestions.q: The first engine should generally stage:
choices: Upwind/uphill/upstream of the problem as conditions allow
Against the tank for a good photo
On the downhill side to ‘catch runoff’ with the crew
readinessQuestions.why: Apparatus are not plugs for a plume.

skills.title: ERG Navigation
skills.summary: Find the material, the guide, isolation information, and emergency contacts quickly in the current ERG.
skills.whyItMatters: A reference you cannot navigate under stress is a paperweight.
learningPoints: Know yellow/blue lookup vs orange guides vs green isolation table — in the current edition.
Tablets and apps are fine if they are the current official content.
The ERG is first-responder general guidance, not a site-specific plan.
Practice timed lookups.
beforeYouDo: A current ERG (print or official digital).

terminology.meaning: The orange-bordered general hazard and action information in the ERG.

safetyNotes: Do not use a 10-year-old book in the cab as if it were current.
Apps must be the real current data, not a random screenshot.

drill.objective: Complete timed ERG lookups: name, UN number, placard, and a rail/highway ID — then state the isolation concept.
drill.equipment: Current ERG for every participant, timer, ID list.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Open to the how-to-use section and point to lookup paths.
debrief: Print or digital — is it current?

15.title: 15-minute timed lookups
15.instructions: Ten IDs. Score accuracy, not swagger.
debrief: Which lookup was slowest?

30.title: 30-minute mixed traffic
30.instructions: Combine ERG with a map isolation for two incidents, including a ‘not in the book’ facility chemical.
debrief: Who do we call next?

readinessQuestions.q: If the chemical is a facility product not in the ERG:
choices: Use occupancy procedures, SDS/facility staff, and specialists — do not fake an ERG ID
readinessQuestions.why: The ERG is not every chemical on earth.

readinessQuestions.q: Green-section isolation ideas are:
choices: A starting protective-action tool for certain listed materials/scenarios in the current book
readinessQuestions.why: Read the current table’s conditions.

readinessQuestions.q: Using last decade’s ERG is:
choices: A risk — isolation and guides change; use the current official edition
Better because you marked it up
readinessQuestions.why: Currency is part of competence.

skills.title: Control Zones
skills.summary: Lay out hot/warm/cold concepts so work, decon, and command do not share the same puddle.
skills.whyItMatters: If the cold zone is in the product, everyone is in the hot zone and nobody admitted it.
learningPoints: Zones are about contamination control and access, not pretty tape.
Decon usually lives in the warm zone conceptually.
Command and staging belong out of the product and preferably upwind.
Zones move if the plume or spill moves.

terminology.meaning: Where the hazard is — entry limited to appropriate PPE and mission.

safetyNotes: Do not put rehab in the vapor.
Spectators will walk through tape. Staff the control points.

drill.objective: Using cones or a map, lay out operational zones, access control, decon placement, and command for a defensive incident.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Place command, staging, and a public control point on a sketch.
debrief: Where do ambulances park?

15.title: 15-minute cone drill
debrief: How does a victim get to EMS without contaminating the cold zone?

30.title: 30-minute moving plume
30.instructions: Shift wind 90 degrees. Move zones and explain who is now contaminated.
commonMistakes: Pride in the original tape line
debrief: Who got exposed during the move?

readinessQuestions.q: Command post in the visible vapor is:
readinessQuestions.why: Support belongs in the cold zone.

readinessQuestions.q: Decon is conceptually part of:
choices: Contamination reduction — typically the warm-zone function
readinessQuestions.why: Ops-level decon support still needs a place to exist.

readinessQuestions.q: If the spill grows, zones should:
choices: Only be drawn on a whiteboard downtown
readinessQuestions.why: Geometry follows the product.

skills.title: Emergency Decontamination
skills.summary: Set up operations-level emergency/gross decon so people and equipment do not spread the problem.
skills.whyItMatters: The second incident is the contaminated ambulance and the exposed firefighter who ‘only stepped in it.’
learningPoints: Emergency decon for life safety vs technical decon for a planned entry — know which you are doing.
Flow: dirty to cleaner, not a maze.
Protect decon members with appropriate PPE and a plan for their own decon.
Runoff is a secondary release.

terminology.meaning: Rapid contamination reduction, often for victims or unexpectedly contaminated responders.

safetyNotes: Do not send contaminated patients through a normal ED entrance without notice.

drill.objective: Lay out an operations-level decon corridor with zones, flow, assignments, and a runoff/containment idea.
drill.equipment: Department decon cache or cones/tarp stand-ins, water if authorized, radios.
drill.setup: Do not create a real environmental release. Contain training water.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Sketch dirty-to-clean flow and where EMS waits.
debrief: Where do clothes go?

15.title: 15-minute corridor
15.instructions: Build it with cones. Assign wash, bagging, and a medic in the cold zone.
debrief: How do we decon the decon team?

30.title: 30-minute victim flow
30.instructions: Two ambulatory and one non-ambulatory cards. Keep contamination out of the ambulance.
commonMistakes: Loading a dirty patient because it is faster
debrief: What does the hospital need to hear?

readinessQuestions.q: The point of emergency decon is:
choices: Rapidly reduce contamination to protect life and keep the rest of the system clean
readinessQuestions.why: Speed and isolation, not spa day.

readinessQuestions.q: A contaminated patient in an unprotected ambulance:
choices: Spreads the incident into the hospital system
Is fine if windows are down
readinessQuestions.why: Notify and protect the chain of care.

readinessQuestions.q: Runoff from decon:
choices: Can be a secondary contamination problem — plan containment per SOP
Should go to storm drains by default
readinessQuestions.why: You can make a second spill.

skills.title: Defensive Control Options
skills.summary: Choose defensive actions you are trained and authorized to do: dike, dam, divert, remote valve, vapor suppression — and stop at the ops boundary.
skills.whyItMatters: Operations level is not ‘almost a technician.’ Leaving your level is how people die in product.
learningPoints: Defensive means you are not plugging the hole with your body in a Level A suit unless that is actually your qualification.
Remote shutoff and product control that does not require entering the release are the usual wins.
Diking buys time for people who own the product.
If you cannot explain the action inside your SOP, do not do it.

terminology.meaning: Preventing spread and protecting people/environment without offensive leak control beyond your training.
Entry and leak control requiring higher qualification and PPE.

safetyNotes: A boom in a fast sewer can become a drowning/confined hazard.
Vapor suppression foam is a foam problem plus a HazMat problem.

practiceResources.label: Foam Operations skill
practiceResources.note: If vapor suppression is the tool.

drill.objective: For a spill scenario, pick defensive options within ops-level authorization, list required equipment, and name the stop point.
drill.equipment: Scenario cards, cones for a dike line, department absorbent/boom if available.
drill.setup: No real product. Discuss environmental notifications.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: List five defensive options and one action that would be technician-only on your team.
debrief: Who owns the facility valve?

15.title: 15-minute spill
15.instructions: 50-gallon drum leak toward a drain. Plan dike/divert and notifications.
commonMistakes: Standing in the product to place a pad
debrief: Do we have enough boom?

30.title: 30-minute mixed incident
30.instructions: Leak plus fire plus a crowd. Prioritize life, isolation, then product. Call the boundary when the problem needs a team.
debrief: What did we tell the technician team?

readinessQuestions.q: An operations-level firefighter should:
choices: Enter any cloud if the officer is excited
Take defensive actions they are trained and authorized for, and request technicians when the job exceeds that
Never touch a valve even if it is a labeled remote shutoff they are trained to use
readinessQuestions.why: Train and SOP define the box.

readinessQuestions.q: Stopping product from entering a storm drain is usually:
choices: A common defensive goal using dikes/covers you are trained to use
readinessQuestions.why: Keep it out of the water system.

readinessQuestions.q: If the only ‘fix’ requires entering the release in chemical PPE you do not have:
choices: Hold isolation, protect people, and get the right team
readinessQuestions.why: Structural firefighting gear is not a chemically resistant suit.

skills.title: PPE Limitations
skills.summary: Know what department HazMat PPE actually protects against — and when structural firefighting gear is the wrong answer.
skills.whyItMatters: The wrong suit is a costume. Breakthrough, heat stress, and training limits kill.
learningPoints: Structural PPE is for fire, not a chemical catalog.
Chemical protective clothing is chemical- and manufacturer-specific.
Heat stress in encapsulating suits is a medical problem.
If you are not trained and medically cleared for the ensemble, you do not wear it to ‘help.’
beforeYouDo: What CPC/SCBA combinations YOUR department actually fields at ops level.
Manufacturer lookup culture — do not memorize a 1990s chart as gospel.

terminology.meaning: When a chemical moves through a material — time is not infinite.

safetyNotes: Never assume dish soap and a rain coat are chemical PPE.
Decon the people who wore the suits.

drill.objective: Review department PPE: what it is for, what it is not for, and when specialist guidance is required.
drill.equipment: Department HazMat PPE (display), manufacturer info, scenario cards.
drill.setup: Do not make untrained members don technician ensembles.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Name three chemicals or conditions where structural gear is the wrong answer.
debrief: Who is medically cleared to wear CPC?

15.title: 15-minute ensemble talk
15.instructions: Match three scenarios to no-entry vs ops PPE vs tech team.
commonMistakes: Dressing the volunteer in Level A for photos
debrief: What is our heat-stress plan?

30.title: 30-minute don/doff if authorized
30.instructions: Only for members already in the program: inspect, don, walk, emergency doff concept, decon path.
debrief: Where does contaminated CPC go?

readinessQuestions.q: Structural firefighting clothing in a chemical vapor:
choices: Is generally the wrong ensemble unless the AHJ and the hazard say otherwise
readinessQuestions.why: It is fire gear.

readinessQuestions.q: Chemical suit selection must consider:
choices: The chemical, concentration, manufacturer data, and mission time
readinessQuestions.why: There is no universal suit.

readinessQuestions.q: If you are not trained in the ensemble:
choices: Wear it anyway to be brave
Do not wear it — request qualified members
readinessQuestions.why: Untrained CPC is a hazard.

skills.title: HazMat Initial Radio Brief
skills.summary: Give a concise first report: location, clues, wind, exposures, actions, resources, and a safe approach.
skills.whyItMatters: The second-due company will drive into the product if your first report was ‘we have a smell.’
learningPoints: Name the problem class if known, and the uncertainty if not.
Give an approach/staging instruction.
Say what you are doing (isolate, deny entry) and what you need (HazMat team, PD, public works).
Keep it short enough to hear.

terminology.meaning: Where later units should come from — usually upwind/uphill.

safetyNotes: Do not transmit guesses as facts.
If people are down, say so — that changes everything.

practiceResources.label: HazMat Size-Up Checklist
practiceResources.note: Build the report from a list.

practiceResources.label: Fire Officer I — initial radio report

drill.objective: Deliver a 20–30 second HazMat initial report from a photo, including approach instructions.
drill.equipment: Photos, radios or timer, size-up checklist.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: List the must-have pieces of the first transmission.
debrief: Where should Engine 2 stop?

15.title: 15-minute photo reports
15.instructions: Five photos, 25 seconds each. Partner scores missing pieces.
debrief: Would you have driven into it?

30.title: 30-minute evolving leak
30.instructions: Report, then a wind shift and a victim. Second report and resource request.
debrief: When does this become a mass-casualty problem?

readinessQuestions.q: The most important extra in a HazMat first report vs a house fire is often:
readinessQuestions.why: Later units need a place to not die.

readinessQuestions.q: If you do not know the product, you should:
choices: Make up a UN number to sound sure
Say what clues you have and what you do not know
readinessQuestions.why: Uncertainty is useful information.

readinessQuestions.q: ‘People down’ in the first report:
choices: Is a priority piece of information
Means you should enter immediately in bunker gear
readinessQuestions.why: Life hazard changes the whole response — still do not create more victims.
